definition: A tool that keeps a history of every change to your project so you can go back in time, compare versions, or work with others.
analogy: Like 'Track Changes' in a document, but for an entire folder of files.

definition: A saved checkpoint of your project with a short message describing what changed.
analogy: Saving a named version of a document you can always return to.

definition: Uploads your saved checkpoints to an online copy of the project (usually GitHub).
analogy: Syncing your local folder to the cloud.

definition: Downloads changes other people (or other machines) have uploaded so your copy is up to date.
Checks the online copy for new changes without applying them yet.
A separate line of work so you can try something without touching the main version.
analogy: Making a copy of a document to experiment in, then merging the good parts back.

definition: The primary, 'official' version of the project that other branches are compared against.
Combines the work from one branch into another.
Replays your changes on top of the latest version of another branch to keep history tidy.
A side-by-side view of exactly which lines were added or removed.
analogy: A red-pen markup showing what changed between two drafts.

definition: A compact summary of the diff: how many lines changed in each file, rather than the lines themselves.
Lists which files have been changed, added, or deleted since the last checkpoint.
analogy: A quick health check: 'what's different right now?'

definition: In a status list, 'M' marks a file that already existed and has been edited.
In a status list, '??' marks a brand-new file that git isn't watching yet.
Changes you've selected to include in the next checkpoint.
analogy: Putting items in a shopping basket before checking out.

definition: The list of past checkpoints, newest first, each with its message and a short ID.
A short code like 'fa473f0' that uniquely identifies one checkpoint.
The online copy of your project. 'origin' is the default nickname for it.
Moves your working files to a different branch or an older checkpoint.
Temporarily sets aside your uncommitted changes so you can come back to them later.
Downloads a complete copy of a project, including its history.
A website that hosts git projects online so people can share, back up, and review code.
A request to merge one branch into another, usually with review and discussion.
A list of files git should ignore, like downloaded libraries or secret settings.
A text window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons.
analogy: Talking to your computer in short typed sentences.

definition: A single instruction typed into the terminal, like 'ls' (list files) or 'git status'.
An extra switch on a command that tweaks how it behaves, like '-n' for 'show line numbers'.
Runs several commands in a row; each one only runs if the previous one succeeded.
Sends the output of one command into another, e.g. 'list files | count them'.
The text a command prints back after running.
A number a command returns when it finishes: 0 means success, anything else means something went wrong.
The folder the terminal is currently 'standing in'; commands act relative to it.
The address of a file, like 'src/styles/global.css' — folders separated by slashes.
Lists the files in a folder.
Prints a file's contents to the terminal. 'head' shows the beginning, 'tail' the end.
A very fast text search across every file in a project.
analogy: Ctrl+F for your entire project at once.

definition: A compact search pattern. For example 'home-field|data-home-field' means 'either of these two phrases'.
Files whose names start with a dot (like .env) are hidden by default; this flag includes them.
A file-name pattern with wildcards, e.g. '*.css' means 'every file ending in .css'.
The folder where downloaded third-party code (libraries) lives. Usually huge and safe to ignore.
Fetches a web page or API response from the terminal, often to check that a server is responding.
Your own computer acting as a web server so you can preview a site before publishing it.
A local preview of your site that refreshes automatically as files change.
A tool that downloads and manages the third-party code (packages) your project depends on.
analogy: An app store for code building blocks.

definition: A bundle of reusable code written by someone else that your project uses, like GSAP or React.
The project's settings file: its name, the packages it needs, and shortcut commands (scripts).
A named shortcut in package.json, like 'npm run build', that runs a longer command.
Runs a command from a package without permanently installing it.
Turns your source files into the optimized files a browser actually loads.
An automatic proofreader that flags likely mistakes or style problems in code.
Verifies that the pieces of code fit together correctly before running anything.
Small automatic checks that confirm code still behaves as expected after changes.
A named setting (often a secret like an API key) kept outside the code.
Changes who is allowed to read, edit, or run a file.
A command left running (like a dev server) while other work continues.
The human-written instructions that make up your project. Usually lives in a 'src' folder.
A targeted change that swaps one exact block of text in a file for another.
The language that defines the structure and content of a web page: headings, paragraphs, images.
The language that controls how a page looks: colors, spacing, fonts, layout, animation.
The programming language that makes web pages interactive.
JavaScript with added labels ('types') that catch mistakes early. Files end in .ts or .tsx.
A reusable building block of a page (a button, a card, a header) with its own markup, style, and logic.
Settings passed into a component to customize it, like the text on a button.
A named chunk of code that does one job and can be reused.
A named container for a value the code can refer to later.
A line at the top of a file that pulls in code from another file or package.
A named value like --surface reused across styles so one change updates everything.
The part of a CSS rule that says which elements it applies to, e.g. '.card'.
A CSS rule that only applies at certain screen sizes or user preferences.
A user setting that asks websites to tone down animation; good sites respect it.
Making things on the page move or change over time.
Starting each item's animation slightly after the previous one, creating a ripple effect.
The live, in-memory tree of everything on the page that JavaScript can read and change.
A defined way for two programs to talk to each other, e.g. your site asking a server for data.
A plain-text format for structured data, using {curly braces} and "quotes". Used for settings and API responses.
A file with one JSON record per line — handy for logs and transcripts.
A lightweight way to write formatted text with plain characters (# for headings, ** for bold).
A human-friendly settings format using indentation. Often appears at the top of Markdown files as 'frontmatter'.
A ready-made structure for building apps so you don't start from scratch. Astro, React, and Next.js are examples.
Making sure people using assistive tech (screen readers, keyboards only) can use the site.
Reorganizing code so it's cleaner without changing what it does.
A mistake that makes the code behave incorrectly. An 'error' is the message that reveals it.
Hunting down why something isn't working, often by printing values or stepping through code.
The AI assistant in Cursor that can read files, run commands, and edit code on your behalf.
One action the agent takes, like reading a file, searching, or running a command.
One round of conversation: your message plus everything the agent does in response.
A helper agent the main agent spins up to handle a focused job (like exploring the codebase) in parallel.
A mode where the agent only researches and proposes a plan; it doesn't change files until you approve.
The agent's own checklist of steps for the current task, updated as it works.
A reusable instruction guide the agent reads to do a specific kind of task well (e.g. 'GSAP animations').
Standing instructions that shape how the agent behaves in a project.
A plug-in system that lets the agent use outside services (Figma, Slack, a database) as tools.
A small script that runs automatically at certain moments in the agent's work, e.g. after every command.
The saved record of a chat, including every tool call the agent made.
Everything the agent can currently 'see': your messages, files it has read, and results so far.
The message you send the agent.
The underlying AI brain the agent uses to think and write.
The agent looking up documentation or facts online before acting.
The agent opening a real browser tab to click around and verify a page works.
A live visual panel the agent can build beside the chat for charts, reports, or tools.
An add-on that gives the editor new features, like this Decipher panel.
The folder you have open in Cursor — your whole project.
